opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and I'd frame it honestly: it's useful today, but you have to be thoughtful about where you point it.

The way I think about it, there's a spectrum of coding tasks. On one end you have well-scoped, verifiable work: fix this bug where there's a failing test, add this endpoint following the patterns already in the repo, write tests for this module, do this refactor across a bunch of files. For that category, an agent running in your terminal that can read the codebase, run commands, execute the tests, and iterate is genuinely ready. People are getting real value from it right now, and the key ingredient is that feedback loop. When the model can run the code and see what breaks, its reliability goes up a lot compared to just generating code in a chat window.

On the other end you have tasks that are ambiguous, where the hard part isn't writing the code but figuring out what should be built, or where the right answer depends on context that isn't written down anywhere. Why is this system designed this way, what does the team care about, what are the unstated constraints. That's where you still need a human pretty heavily in the loop. The model will produce something plausible, but plausible isn't the same as right.

So my practical advice is: treat it like a capable new teammate. Give it clear tasks, make sure your repo has good tests and a way to run them, maybe write down some conventions in an instructions file so it knows how your project works, and review the output the way you'd review a pull request. Teams that invest in making their codebase legible to an agent see dramatically better results than teams that just drop it in and hope.

And the trajectory matters too. The jump in what these agents can do autonomously over the past year or so has been significant, and the length of task they can reliably complete keeps growing. So even if today the sweet spot is tasks that take a person maybe an hour or two, I'd expect that window to keep expanding. The teams building those habits now are going to be well positioned as it does.

r001.rationale: The response says Codex CLI can handle well-scoped coding tasks and act like a capable teammate, but it does not state that it helps developers complete work beyond their existing knowledge or expertise.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the honest answer is that it's a moving target, and the way I think about it has shifted a lot even over the last year. When we first put Codex CLI out, I'd have described it as useful but with a pretty narrow sweet spot: well-scoped tasks, a codebase where the tests are good, a user who's willing to read the diff carefully. If you stayed inside that envelope, it saved you real time. If you stepped outside it, it could make a mess that cost you more than it saved.

The way I actually assess readiness isn't by looking at benchmark numbers, although we do track those. It's by looking at what tasks people are willing to hand off and then walk away from. That's the real signal. Early on, nobody walked away. You'd kick off a task and sit there watching it, because you didn't trust it to not do something weird, like delete a test that was failing instead of fixing the code. The moment people start delegating a task and going to lunch, that's when the thing is actually ready for that class of work.

So I'd break it down roughly into a few buckets. There's the stuff where I think it's clearly past the bar now: refactors with good test coverage, writing tests for existing code, migrating something from one API version to another, fixing a well-described bug where you can point at the failing case. Those are tasks where the agent can verify its own work, and that's the key property. When the model can run something and see whether it succeeded, the whole dynamic changes, because it gets to iterate instead of guessing.

Then there's the middle bucket, which is where most of the interesting work lives. Things like implementing a feature that touches several parts of the system, or anything where the spec is underdetermined. There it's useful, but the quality depends heavily on how much context you give it and how good your repo's feedback loops are. A codebase with a solid test suite, type checking, linting, a clear structure, that's a codebase the agent does well in. A codebase that's a big ball of mud with no tests, the agent struggles in exactly the way a new hire would struggle, except it struggles faster.

And then there's the bucket where I'd say it's still not there: ambiguous architectural decisions, anything where the right answer depends on organizational context that isn't written down anywhere, or long-horizon work where a mistake early on compounds over hours. The models are getting better at long horizons, but the error rate per step still matters a lot when you multiply it over a few hundred steps.

The other thing I'd add is that readiness isn't only a property of the model. A lot of what we've learned building the CLI is that the harness matters enormously. How the agent explores the repo, how it manages context, whether it gets to run things in a sandbox, how it recovers when a command fails. Two products with the same underlying model can feel very different in terms of readiness, because one of them gives the model the feedback loops it needs and the other doesn't. So when I'm assessing it, I'm really assessing the whole system, and a lot of our investment has been on that side rather than purely waiting for the next model.

I guess if you forced me to summarize it: it's genuinely useful today for a large and growing class of tasks, it's most useful in codebases that are already set up to give good feedback, and the frontier of what you can delegate is moving faster than most people's intuitions about it. The failure mode I see most often isn't people trusting it too much, it's people who tried it a year ago, got burned, and haven't updated.

r001.rationale: The response describes Codex CLI completing coding tasks and when it is useful, but does not say it helps developers work beyond their existing knowledge or expertise.

astra-6.text:
I’d assess it by looking at whether it can take a real task in an existing codebase and produce a change that a developer would actually accept. Can it find the relevant code, understand the constraints, make the change, and verify that it works? And how much intervention does it need along the way?

There’s a big difference between being useful and being ready to operate autonomously. A tool can be useful even if you need to review every change, provided it saves you more time than you spend checking and correcting it. So I’d want to see results on representative tasks, including the failures and the amount of supervision required, before making a strong claim about readiness.

r001.rationale: The response says Codex CLI can handle real coding tasks and save developer time, but does not say it helps developers work beyond their existing knowledge or expertise.

sol-6.1.text: I’d assess it by putting it to work on real tasks in a real codebase. Can it understand the relevant context, make a change, run the tests, and respond intelligently when something fails? And then, how much supervision did that require? Getting to a plausible patch is useful, but the bigger question is whether reviewing and correcting that patch takes less effort than doing the work yourself. I’d also distinguish between being useful with a developer in the loop and being ready to handle a task autonomously. Those are very different bars.

r001.rationale: The response describes assessing Codex CLI on real coding tasks and measuring supervision, but does not say it helps developers complete work beyond their existing knowledge or expertise.
